headline: Pure steam that passes EN 285 dryness, superheat and non-condensable gas tests at the sterilizer
lead: Our pure steam generators supply autoclaves and steam-in-place (SIP) with steam whose condensate meets Water for Injection (WFI) limits, as EU GMP Annex 1 paragraph 6.17 requires, and whose non-condensable gases (no more than 3.5 mL per 100 mL of condensate), dryness and superheat meet EN 285 where the steam is used. We size the generator and the distribution header as one system, because most steam quality failures start in the pipework, and we hand over the test records your validation team needs.

blocks.h: Pure steam is qualified on two sets of tests, and only one is about the generator
body: Pure steam sterilizes product-contact surfaces directly: porous and hard-goods loads in autoclaves, vessels and transfer lines by SIP, and stoppers in processors. EU GMP Annex 1 (2022), adopted by Health Canada as GUI-0119 and in force since 1 April 2024, sets two requirements for it in paragraph 6.17. The condensate must meet the current WFI monograph of the relevant pharmacopoeia, with microbial testing not mandatory. And the steam must be assessed periodically for non-condensable gases, dryness value and superheat against validated parameters.

The first set is chemistry. USP Pure Steam tests the condensate for total organic carbon (TOC), conductivity and, where the steam is used to make parenterals, bacterial endotoxin (< 0.25 EU/mL). The generator controls these: droplet separation keeps feed water and its endotoxin out of the steam, and feed degassing keeps dissolved carbon dioxide (CO₂) from raising conductivity.

The second set is physics, and EN 285 gives the acceptance criteria most sterilizer manufacturers and inspectors use. These tests are made at the sterilizer. A generator that delivers dry, gas-free steam at its outlet can still fail them at the point of use if the header collects condensate, leaks air in during shutdown, or reduces pressure in one large step. So we design, test and document the generator and its distribution together.

blocks.h: How a pure steam generator works
blocks.caption: PW is preheated and vented, so dissolved air and CO₂ leave before evaporation. Plant steam or electric heaters boil it in the evaporator, on the far side of a double tube sheet. The vapour rises through a separation stage that returns droplets, and the endotoxin and solids they carry, to the evaporator. Pure steam leaves at a controlled pressure, through a sample cooler, to a drained and insulated header. Blowdown removes the concentrated feed.

blocks.h: Questions validation and engineering teams ask

items.q: You are a new firm. How do you back your FAT and SAT results without an installed base?
items.a: With evidence you can check rather than references: a FAT protocol your quality unit approves, a witnessed test on steam, test instruments with calibration certificates in the report and the raw readings in the executed protocol. At SAT we test steam quality at the sterilizer, where EN 285 is judged, not only at the generator.

items.q: What happens if our steam fails EN 285 at the sterilizer during commissioning?
items.a: We size the generator and the header together, so a header problem is ours to find. We check traps, separators, slope, insulation and pressure reduction, correct them and test again. [Confirm commissioning scope: header correction and retest included or quoted separately.]

items.q: Our sterilizer fails the dryness test. Is it the generator?
items.a: Usually it is the header. Condensate that collects in flat or sagging runs, missing or failed traps, damaged insulation and dead legs all produce wet steam at the sterilizer from a generator that tests dry at its outlet. We survey the header and the generator together, test at the generator and at the sterilizer, and the difference tells you where the water comes from.

items.q: Does the condensate really have to meet WFI?
items.a: For steam that sterilizes materials or product-contact surfaces directly, yes: Annex 1 paragraph 6.17 asks for condensate that meets the current WFI monograph, without microbial testing. USP Pure Steam applies its < 0.25 EU/mL endotoxin limit when the steam is used to make parenterals. Steam that only heats jackets or coils, without product contact, can be plant steam; your contamination control strategy should say which users are which.

items.q: EN 285 is a European sterilizer standard. Does it apply to us?
items.a: EN 285 is written for large steam sterilizers, and its steam quality clause gives the acceptance criteria for gases, dryness and superheat. Annex 1, which Health Canada applies as GUI-0119, names the same three parameters but sets no numbers, so most sites and sterilizer manufacturers use the EN 285 values. If your sterilizer manufacturer specifies different limits, we design to the stricter of the two.

items.q: How often do we have to test?
items.a: Annex 1 asks for a sampling schedule that obtains representative steam regularly and for periodic assessment of the physical parameters. It sets no interval. A common approach is condensate chemistry and endotoxin quarterly, non-condensable gases quarterly until the data support a longer interval, dryness annually, and superheat watched continuously from pressure and temperature. Your validation plan sets the actual frequency.

items.q: What feed water does the generator need?
items.a: USP allows pure steam to be made from drinking water, but feed impurities concentrate in the evaporator. Silica and hardness scale the heat transfer surface, chloride attacks stainless steel at these temperatures, and CO₂ and ammonia raise condensate conductivity. We feed from PW or RO permeate and write the feed limits into the functional specification, so blowdown and cleaning intervals are predictable.

Mostly from reducing the pressure of dry saturated steam in one large step, or through a small orifice close to the sterilizer. Superheated steam behaves like hot air until it cools to saturation, so sterilization is less effective. We stage pressure reduction and place it far enough upstream for the steam to return to saturation before the sterilizer.

items.q: Can we use our WFI still instead of a separate generator?
items.a: Often, yes. The first column of a multi-effect still can deliver pure steam, with WFI output reduced while it does. It suits small or intermittent steam demand. A separate generator is the better choice when sterilizers and SIP run while WFI demand is high, or when you want to maintain one without stopping the other.

items.q: Does an imported generator need a Canadian registration number?
items.a: Yes. Pressure vessels and fittings installed in Canada need a CRN under CSA B51 from the province of installation, and a generator designed for another market may need design changes before it is accepted. We include registration in the project schedule from the start. [Confirm Aquemi's CRN process and the provinces covered.]
